dossier.public_summary: The dip changes depth dramatically between sectors and even disappears, with individual transits showing no consistent depth. The light also shows a strong wobble at the same period and an unusually long duration for this star, all indicating the star's own variability rather than a planet. The signal is on the target itself, so it is not a background eclipsing binary, just stellar activity mimicking a transit.

reasons.why: Depth changes by a factor of ~2-3 and even reverses sign (negative depths in sectors 79/80) within the same pipeline (SPOC 2-min). The p_constant is astronomically low, indicating the dip is not steady as required for a planet on the target.
reasons.value: changes_within_a_source, p_constant 1.214e-203, SPOC 2-min p_constant 1.8431059913105297e-105, depth change 251.6%, sectors 25 depth_ppm 11442, sector 26 depth_ppm 12962, sector 52 depth_ppm 6652, sector 53 depth_ppm 9926, sector 79 depth_ppm -2568, sector 80 depth_ppm -1380

reasons.why: Individual transits are inconsistent with a single depth; negative outliers show dips that are actually brightenings in some events, inconsistent with a uniform transit.
Large phase-curve swing at this period (~48% of the transit depth) with high chi2 points to stellar variability/spot modulation or a close binary, not a quiet planet host.

Duration is ~60% longer than central for this K dwarf and star density ratio rejects a planet density; combined with variable star and large phase signal favours astrophysical variability over a planet.
reasons.value: duration ratio 1.629 (1.6 for Gaia radii), fit_log_density_ratio -1.837, phase-curve large, RUWE 1.083, VARIABLE flag

reasons.why: Centroid is on target with no plausible neighbours that can cause the dip, so the variable signal is intrinsic to the target, not a blended binary, supporting stellar variability as the best explanation.
